source.title: Improving the Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM) stochastic optimizer through an Implicit-Explicit (IMEX) time-stepping approach
source.authors: Abhinab Bhattacharjee; Andrey A. Popov; A. Sarshar; Adrian Sandu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares standard ADAM and SGD and reports held-out classification performance, using a different optimizer comparison from the claim’s cited studies.
record.gate_note: The authors state that their experiments focus on minimizing training cost, not generalization, though they report test losses in several cases. The only explicit held-out comparison relevant to V4 is CIFAR-10 with VGG: the text says all three methods have about the same test accuracy. Other optimizer performance curves are not held-out generalization results.
record.test_reason: The CIFAR-10 experiment directly compares held-out accuracy for SGD and an Adam implementation, bearing on V4 despite the paper's primary focus on training-loss minimization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors interpret Adam as an IMEX Euler discretization and propose higher-order extensions. They favor IMEX Trapezoidal for its balance of training-loss reduction and gradient-evaluation cost, reporting advantages on Lorenz63, sum-of-Gaussians, and Swiss-roll tasks, but little computational advantage over Adam on MNIST and CIFAR-10. They do not conclude that it generally improves held-out generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces and evaluates an IMEX time-stepping optimizer against ADAM and SGD; it does not use the original claim’s memorization, generalization-gap, or optimizer-tuning protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and architecture: the authors report that the new method offers little computational advantage on MNIST and CIFAR-10, while it outperforms standard ADAM in some regression and Swiss roll experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: The MNIST accuracy pairs compare Adam with the proposed IMEX Trapezoidal method: 94.7% versus 94.7%, 94.27% versus 94.45%, and 94.56% versus 94.43%. No corresponding held-out SGD accuracy is supplied.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The proposed higher-order Adam variant achieves similar MNIST accuracy to the paper's first-order Adam implementation across three hyperparameter settings.

record.problems: The paper says its experiments focus on minimizing training cost rather than generalization. Held-out optimizer comparisons are limited, and the CIFAR-10 result is qualitative with no exact accuracy values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional explicit held-out optimizer comparison appears in the supplied text. Training-loss curves and results about convergence speed are not rows for the generalization claim.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out performance under the same architecture and recipe.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.

The frequency of adaptive-optimizer disadvantages across benchmarks; language modeling; controlled comparisons of restricted versus broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; and switching from Adam to SGD. The reported grid search does not establish the claim's specific limited-tuning protocol.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Held-out effects of adding or removing dropout.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing highly memorized examples versus randomly selected examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 8b and Section 4.5 explicitly concern held-out accuracy. Figure 8's statement that the IMEX methods outperform SGD should not override the explicit approximately equal test-accuracy statement; the training-loss comparison favors the IMEX methods. Numerical stability analyses and training-loss curves do not measure the sharpness–generalization relationship in V7.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold and test error.
The paper does not systematically compare adaptive optimizers with SGD across image and language benchmarks, tune optimizer schedules as described, or test weight decay and optimizer switching.
Large-batch effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Sharpness or other measured properties as predictors of the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: VGG-16
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD, IMEX ADAM, and IMEX Trapezoidal on CIFAR-10; reported test accuracy.
rows.value: All three methods show about the same accuracy on the test dataset.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison, not exact accuracy values. The comparison includes IMEX ADAM, not only standard ADAM.
rows.check: The qualitative accuracy comparison is correctly recorded. However, 'batches = 100' denotes the number of batches, not a batch size of 100. Describe the comparator as the paper's IMEX Adam implementation: experiments initialize velocity to the squared initial gradient, and Appendix A omits bias correction. The IMEX Trapezoidal comparison evaluates the proposed method and supplies no independent evidence about the usual Adam–SGD generalization difference.

relationships.condition: VGG-16 on CIFAR-10, learning rate 0.001, 100 batches, using the paper's Adam implementation.
relationships.reason: R1 reports approximately equal held-out accuracy for SGD and IMEX Adam, providing a setting without an adaptive-optimizer penalty; unspecified grid-search scope and implementation differences limit its bearing on the limited-tuning claim.
relationships.display_finding: IMEX Adam reportedly achieved approximately equal held-out accuracy, but the comparison remains unverified and implementation and tuning differences complicate interpretation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
